# Support Audit — full text

> Independent resident support file audits for supported exempt accommodation (SEA)
> and transitional supported housing in England. Every finding names the document,
> the date and what good looks like. Files are rated Gold, Green, Amber or Red.
> Contact: contact@supportaudit.co.uk

## Support Audit | Supported Exempt Accommodation Audits
Source: https://supportaudit.co.uk/

Are your files ready? Resident support files that stand up to scrutiny. Support Audit carries out independent audits of resident support files in supported exempt accommodation. Every finding names the document, the date and what good looks like, and every file gets a clear Gold, Green, Amber or Red rating your team can act on. Support Audit is an independent audit service for supported exempt accommodation (SEA) and transitional supported housing in England. We review resident support files (assessments, support plans, risk assessments, session notes and reviews) against your own standards and the National Supported Housing Standards, then report what is working, what is missing and exactly how to fix it. 4 bands Gold, Green, Amber or Red, with the reason for every rating 5 parts Checklist, evidence, support delivered, strengths and next steps 10 documents Core records checked in every resident file 2027 When supported housing licensing is expected to begin Our approach Every finding names the document , the date and what good looks like . Every file gets a clear rating and the reason for it. Strengths are named as specifically as gaps, because the point is improvement . Why now Licensing is coming. Evidence is what will count. Supported exempt accommodation is moving to national standards and local licences. Providers who can show their support, file by file, will be ready for it. 01 National standards, local licences The Supported Housing (Regulatory Oversight) Act 2023 lets government set National Supported Housing Standards and require a local licence to run supported exempt accommodation. Meeting the standards becomes a licence condition. 02 Housing Benefit tied to the licence In its April 2026 response, government confirmed it will amend Housing Benefit regulations so that enhanced Housing Benefit in England is linked to the new licensing regime. 03 A short window to prepare Government expects to consult on draft regulations in late 2026, with licensing expected from 2027. Local supported housing strategies are due by 31 March 2027. Read our plain-English guide to supported housing licensing What we check Ten documents. One standard. Scroll to move through the file 01 Referral form Why the resident was referred and by whom. Every question answered, signed and dated. 02 Admission form The start of the stay and what the resident was told, signed on the move-in day. 03 Licence agreement The right landlord or agent name, address and rent, signed by both parties. 04 Needs assessment Completed within four weeks of move-in and kept current as things change. 05 Support plan Goals that follow from assessed needs, specific to the person and agreed with them. 06 Risk assessment Each risk scored and described, consistent with the rest of the file. 07 Risk management plans A current, dated plan for every risk that scores high enough to need one. 08 Session notes Regular, dated, linked to a goal, showing the support given and the progress made. 09 Reviews At 3, 6 and 9 months, signed by the resident and staff, with goals updated. 10 Exit or move-on form Completed whenever a resident leaves, with the outcome and forwarding details. Who it's for One audit standard for both sides of the arrangement. Registered Providers Managing agents and support providers Independent oversight of every managing agent. You hold the lease and the accountability. When licensing arrives, you will need confidence that the support delivered in your homes meets the standards. We give you a consistent, evidence-based view of how each managing agent is supporting your residents, and what needs to change. Talk about audit rounds Talk about audit rounds Audit rounds per managing agent, covering every resident file in scope A report for each resident, plus overall feedback for the agent Ratings and open actions tracked from one round to the next A follow-up call 4 to 8 weeks later to check progress Know where your files stand before anyone else checks. Your Registered Provider, the council and soon a licensing team will all want evidence. A Mock Audit shows you what they would find, and how to fix it, while there is still time. A structured checklist means every file is checked the same way. An experienced auditor reads every file, makes every judgement and sets every grade. 01 Scope 02 Secure transfer 03 Review 04 Report 05 Improve 01 Scope A short call to agree which files are in scope, which standards apply and your timescale. We confirm a fixed fee before anything starts. 02 Secure transfer You share the resident files for the review period through a secure transfer. Only the files in scope are requested, and everything is handled as special category data. 03 Review Every file is checked against the same structured checklist: signatures, dates, reviews, risk plans and support hours, line by line. The auditor then reads each file as a whole, makes every judgement and sets every grade. 04 Report Each resident gets a rating with a reason, evidence for every finding, the strengths we found and practical next steps. Managing agents also get an overall feedback report. 05 Improve We debrief with your team and check progress 4 to 8 weeks later. A re-audit then confirms actions are closed, or monitoring keeps standards steady between rounds. Next: Secure transfer Next: Secure transfer One clear rating per file Gold, Green, Amber or Red. And exactly why. Every resident file is rated against the same key, with a reason for the rating, so you can compare files, agents and rounds at a glance. Gold Complete, signed and current. Support is evidenced against every goal, with practice worth sharing across the service. Share as best practice Green Compliant, with minor improvements to make. Nothing that puts the resident or the arrangement at risk. Minor improvements Amber Gaps that need action within an agreed timescale, such as late reviews, incomplete records, missing risk plans or goals without evidence. Action required Red Reserved for serious concerns, such as support that does not appear to have been delivered, duplicated session notes or key documents missing. Immediate remediation Inside every report Feedback your staff can actually use. No vague comments. Every resident report follows the same five-part structure, so teams know where to look and what to do next. 01 Document checklist A simple pass or action against each core document, with a short note wherever there is an issue. 02 Evidence Each issue names the document, the date and what is wrong, with an example of what good looks like. 03 Support delivered How the resident has been supported towards each goal, drawn from the session notes, with gaps recorded separately. 04 Strengths Good practice named specifically, so it is recognised and repeated rather than lost among the findings. 05 Next steps Practical actions tied to the resident's own goals, with clear timescales. Example finding Amber Risk assessment, 6-month review The 6-month review was due on 12 March and is dated 27 March. The risk management plan for the risk scored 12 (likelihood 3, severity 4) has not been updated since admission. What good looks like The review completed in the month it falls due, signed and dated by the resident and support worker, with every risk that needs a plan carrying a current, dated risk management plan. Please ensure risk management plans are reviewed alongside each 3, 6 and 9-month review. What a good support file contains Use cases Where an independent audit makes the difference. Onboarding a new managing agent A baseline audit in the first months of a new arrangement, so expectations are set on evidence rather than assumption. Short answers to what providers ask most. Anything else, ask us on the call. What does Support Audit do? We audit resident support files in supported exempt accommodation and transitional supported housing. Each file is checked against a set checklist, rated Gold, Green, Amber or Red with a reason, and returned with evidence, strengths and practical next steps. What does SEA stand for? Supported exempt accommodation: supported housing where Housing Benefit can be paid above normal Local Housing Allowance levels because the landlord, or someone acting for it, also provides care, support or supervision. Who do you audit for? Registered Providers who work with managing agents to deliver support, and managing agents or support providers who want an independent check of their own files. Do you visit properties? No. Our audits are desktop reviews of resident records, carried out remotely or at your office. We don't carry out property inspections. Who decides the rating? An experienced auditor. Our audit system makes sure every file is checked the same way, but every judgement and every grade is made by a person, with the reason written down. How often should resident files be audited? Most audit rounds run every six months and cover the records for that review period. Monitoring adds lighter sampling in between, so issues are caught early. Will the feedback be harsh? It will be honest and specific, but the aim is to help teams improve. Strengths are named alongside issues, and every issue comes with an example of what good looks like. Book a call Know where your files stand. Book a 20-minute discovery call. ## Supported Housing Audits: Mock Audit & Rounds | Support Audit
Source: https://supportaudit.co.uk/audits/

Supported Housing Audits: Mock Audit & Rounds | Support Audit Skip to content SEA Audit Support Audit home Audits Use cases Resources About Book a call Book a call Home Audits Use cases Resources About Book a call Book a discovery call Book a discovery call contact@supportaudit.co.uk Home / Audits The audits Resident support file audits, done properly. Three ways to work with us: a one-off Mock Audit, regular audit rounds for Registered Providers, and ongoing monitoring. All three use the same checklist, the same rating key and the same standard of evidence. Every audit is a desktop review of records, carried out remotely or at your office. Book a discovery call Book a discovery call Compare the audits In short What is a resident support file audit? A resident support file audit is an independent check of the records kept for one resident in supported housing. It tests whether the right documents exist, are signed, dated and current, and whether the support recorded matches the resident's assessed needs and goals. The result is a rating, the evidence behind it and the actions needed to improve. Choose your audit Three services, one standard. 01 Start here Mock Audit A fixed-fee review of a sample of resident files, run exactly as a full audit would be. It shows you what a Registered Provider, a council or a licensing team would find, and how to fix it before they look. Best for: managing agents and support providers preparing for licensing, a contract review or their first RP audit round. Ask about a Mock Audit Ask about a Mock Audit What we review A sample of resident files agreed at scoping, covering a mix of new and longer-term residents. What you receive A rated report for every file, a summary of themes across the sample and a prioritised action plan. How it ends A debrief call with your team to walk through the findings and the fixes. Price A fixed fee, agreed in writing before any files are shared. 02 For Registered Providers Audit Rounds Every resident file for a managing agent, audited on a regular cycle, usually every six months. You get findings you can take straight to the agent, and a record of improvement over time. Best for: Registered Providers who lease properties to one or more managing agents and need independent oversight of the support delivered. Talk about audit rounds Talk about audit rounds What we review Every resident file in scope, using the records for the review period only. What you receive A report for each resident, an overall feedback report for each managing agent and an executive summary for your board. Follow-up A progress call with the agent 4 to 8 weeks after the round, then a re-audit at the next round. Price Quoted per round, based on the number of files and agents. 03 Ongoing Monitoring Lighter, regular sampling between full audits. Standards don't drift, late reviews and dropping support hours surface early, and the next round holds no surprises. Best for: providers and Registered Providers who want to stay audit-ready all year, not just in the run-up to an audit. Ask about monitoring Ask about monitoring What we review A rolling sample of files each month, weighted towards files that were Amber or Red last time. What you receive A monthly update on ratings, open actions and anything that needs attention now. Early warning Reviews coming due, support below the minimum and missed sessions without follow-up. Price A monthly subscription, alongside or between audit rounds. Transitional supported housing The same audits apply to transitional housing, typically a stay of six months to two years after homelessness or another crisis. We pay particular attention to move-on planning and to residents moving from exempt accommodation into a transitional pathway. See the use case Side by side Compare the audits. We audit against your own forms and thresholds first. Where you don't have a standard for something, we use recognised good practice and say so. Area What we look for Gaps we often find Referral and admission Forms complete, every question answered, signed and dated by the resident and staff Unanswered questions, missing resident signature Licence or occupancy agreement In the right landlord or managing agent's name, with the correct address and rent, signed and dated Old landlord name, wrong rent after an increase Support needs assessment Completed promptly after move-in, needs recorded clearly and kept current Assessment completed weeks late, needs not updated after a change Support plan and goals Goals that follow from the assessed needs, agreed with the resident and reviewed Generic goals copied between residents Risk assessment Each risk scored for likelihood and severity, reviewed on schedule Scores that don't match the narrative, reviews missed Risk management plans A plan for every risk that scores high enough to need one, with clear actions High-scoring risks with no plan Session notes Regular sessions, each linked to a goal, with the resident's progress recorded Notes that describe contact but not support Support hours At least the minimum hours agreed for the service, evidenced each week Weeks with no recorded support Missed sessions Missed appointments recorded and followed up under your process Missed sessions with no follow-up attempt Reviews Support plan and risk reviews at 3, 6 and 9 months where the resident has been there long enough Reviews completed late or not at all Move-on and exit Move-on planning recorded, and an exit form where the resident has left No exit record, no forwarding outcome Read the full guide to a good resident support file Mapped to the standards Ready for the National Supported Housing Standards. Government confirmed six standards in April 2026. Four of them can be evidenced directly from resident files, and our audits map to each one. Standard What it expects What we evidence from the file Person-centred support Needs assessments, tailored support plans and consistent support Assessment date against move-in, goals that follow from needs, regular sessions Empowerment Residents involved, informed about their support, able to complain Resident signatures, their voice in plans and reviews, complaints information given Environment A safe setting with risk management, managed referrals and repairs reporting Risk assessments and plans, referral records, repairs raised in session notes Staff and safeguarding Trained, checked staff in sufficient numbers Safeguarding concerns recorded and escalated in the file; staff records on request Local need Schemes link to local services and the local supported housing strategy Scheme-level, outside a resident file review Statement of purpose A clear ethos, aims and outcomes, reviewed every year Scheme-level, reviewed on request The standards are subject to final regulations. Source: our licensing guide , based on the government response of 16 April 2026. The rating key Every rating comes with a reason. The rating tells you how urgent things are. The reason tells you what to do about it. Rating What it means Typical reasons What happens next Gold Exemplary file Complete, current and signed; support evidenced against every goal Shared as an example of good practice Green Compliant Minor gaps such as a missing date or a thin session note Small fixes, checked at the next round Amber Action required Late reviews, incomplete records, missing risk management plans, goals without evidence of support Actions agreed and checked at the follow-up call Red Immediate remediation Reserved for serious concerns: support that does not appear to have been delivered, duplicated session notes, or key documents missing Raised straight away with the provider and the Registered Provider Before we start What we need from you. After the discovery call we send a short checklist. For each resident in scope, we usually ask for: Referral and admission forms The licence or occupancy agreement Support needs assessment and support plan Risk assessment and any risk management plans Session notes and reviews for the review period Exit or move-on forms, where the resident has left Your own audit forms and rating key, if you have them Questions about the audits Before you book. How much does an audit cost? It depends on the number of files and managing agents in scope. A Mock Audit is a fixed fee, audit rounds are quoted per round and monitoring is a monthly subscription. You always get the price in writing before any files are shared. How long does an audit take? We agree a timescale at the scoping call, based on how many files are in scope and how quickly they can be shared. The clock starts when we have the complete files. Which records do you look at? Only the records for the review period. If a resident has been with you longer, earlier gaps are not counted against the current audit unless you ask us to look further back. Can you audit against our own forms? Yes, and we prefer to. Your forms, thresholds and rating key come first. Where they are silent, we use recognised good practice and say so in the report. Do you visit properties? No. Every audit is a desktop review of resident records, carried out remotely or at your office. We don't carry out property inspections or visit residents. Our files are in a case management system. Does that work? Yes. Exports, PDFs or scanned paper records all work. We agree the format at scoping so nothing has to be re-keyed. What happens to the data afterwards? Resident records are special category data under UK GDPR. We agree a data processing agreement and a retention period with you before anything is shared. How we handle data . Not sure which audit fits? A 20-minute call is usually enough to work it out, and you will leave with a fixed price. ## When to Audit Supported Housing Files | Support Audit
Source: https://supportaudit.co.uk/use-cases/

When to Audit Supported Housing Files | Support Audit Skip to content SEA Audit Support Audit home Audits Use cases Resources About Book a call Book a call Home Audits Use cases Resources About Book a call Book a discovery call Book a discovery call contact@supportaudit.co.uk Home / Use cases Use cases When an independent audit pays for itself. Nine situations where Registered Providers, managing agents and support providers use Support Audit, what we do in each, and what you get at the end. In short When do providers need an independent audit? An independent audit is most useful at moments of change or scrutiny, when you need evidence rather than assurance: 1 Before scrutiny: licensing, a council review, a Housing Benefit query or an RP audit round. 2 At a change: a new managing agent, a lease renewal or a move into transitional housing. 3 After a concern: a complaint, safeguarding issue or serious incident. 4 As routine: six-monthly rounds and monitoring, so standards hold all year. Find your situation Use cases by organisation. All Registered Providers Managing agents and providers Showing 9 of 9 use cases Registered Providers Overseeing several managing agents You lease homes to more than one managing agent, each with its own forms, habits and standards. Recommended: Audit Rounds The situation Reports from each agent look different, so it is hard to compare them or know where the real risks sit. What we do Audit every file in scope against one checklist and one rating key, whichever agent holds it. What you get Like-for-like ratings across agents, the weakest files first, and a record of improvement over time. Managing agents and providers Getting ready for supported housing licensing Licensing is expected from 2027, and meeting the National Supported Housing Standards will be a licence condition. Recommended: Mock Audit The situation You believe your files are in order but have never had them checked independently against the new standards. What we do A Mock Audit of a sample of files, mapped to the four standards that can be evidenced from resident records. What you get A clear list of gaps and fixes while there is still time, and a re-audit to show the improvement. Registered Providers Onboarding a new managing agent A new arrangement starts with good intentions and very little shared evidence. Recommended: Baseline audit, then Audit Rounds The situation You need to know early whether the agent's recording meets your standards, not at the first problem. What we do A baseline audit in the first months, with clear guidance on your forms and what good looks like. What you get Expectations set on evidence, early fixes, and a starting point to measure future rounds against. Registered Providers Renewing or reviewing a lease A lease or management agreement is up for renewal, and the decision needs to rest on more than relationships. Recommended: Audit Rounds or a one-off review The situation You need an objective view of how support has been delivered across the term. What we do Review current files and, where you have them, trends from earlier rounds. What you get An evidence base for renewal, conditions for improvement, or a documented reason to change course. Registered Providers Managing agents and providers After a complaint, safeguarding concern or incident Something has gone wrong, and you need to understand what the records show, calmly and fairly. Recommended: Targeted file review The situation Questions are being asked about one resident or one service, and memories differ. What we do An independent review of the relevant files, reporting only what is documented and when. What you get A factual timeline, the gaps in recording, and practical changes to prevent a repeat. Registered Providers Managing agents and providers Moving from exempt into transitional housing Residents are moving from supported exempt accommodation into a transitional pathway, usually a stay of six months to two years. Recommended: Audit Rounds with move-on focus The situation Records need to show progress towards independence, not only that support took place. What we do Audit the move-on plan, the goals that lead to it and the handover between services. What you get Evidence that each move was planned and supported, and fewer residents falling between services. Registered Providers Board and governance assurance Your board is accountable for services delivered in your name, including by managing agents. Recommended: Audit Rounds with executive summary The situation Board papers rely on agents' own reporting, with little independent challenge. What we do Turn each audit round into a short board summary: ratings, trends, risks and open actions. What you get Independent assurance your board can rely on and question. Managing agents and providers Raising the standard of recording across a team Your support workers do good work, but the notes don't always show it. Recommended: Mock Audit, then Monitoring The situation Recording varies between staff, and good practice isn't shared. What we do Use real findings, anonymised, to show what good looks like for each document and goal. What you get Named strengths to build on, clear examples for staff, and steadier ratings over time. Managing agents and providers Evidencing support for Housing Benefit scrutiny Councils are looking more closely at whether exempt claims show real care, support or supervision. Recommended: Mock Audit The situation A council has asked for evidence of the support behind your claims, or you expect it will. What we do Check that each file shows assessed needs, a plan to meet them and support actually delivered. What you get Files that answer the question before it is asked, and a clear view of any that don't. Recognise your situation? Tell us about it on a 20-minute call. We will tell you honestly whether an audit is the right next step. ## Supported Housing Guides, Glossary & Key Dates | Support Audit
Source: https://supportaudit.co.uk/resources/

Supported Housing Guides, Glossary & Key Dates | Support Audit Skip to content SEA Audit Support Audit home Audits Use cases Resources About Book a call Book a call Home Audits Use cases Resources About Book a call Book a discovery call Book a discovery call contact@supportaudit.co.uk Home / Resources Resources Supported housing, explained plainly. Guides, quick answers, key dates and a glossary for Registered Providers, managing agents and support teams. Every claim links to its primary source. Guides Quick answers Key dates Glossary Sources Guides In-depth guides. Written by auditors, checked against primary sources and reviewed whenever the rules change. Regulation · 12 minute read Supported housing licensing explained What the Supported Housing (Regulatory Oversight) Act 2023 does, what the National Supported Housing Standards say, who will need a licence, what it means for Housing Benefit and when it starts. Read the guide What the 2023 Act does The six National Supported Housing Standards Who needs a licence, and who is exempt Licensing and Housing Benefit Timeline and what to do now Practice · 10 minute read What a good resident support file contains A document-by-document guide to the resident support file: what auditors look for, the gaps we see most often and a worked example of what good looks like for each. Read the guide The ten core documents Evidencing support against goals Risk scoring and risk management plans Reviews at 3, 6 and 9 months A self-check before your next audit Quick answers The questions we are asked most. Short, sourced answers. Follow the guides for the detail. What is supported exempt accommodation? Supported exempt accommodation is housing provided by a housing association, registered charity, voluntary organisation or certain councils, where that body or someone acting for it also provides the resident with care, support or supervision. It is "exempt" because Housing Benefit can be paid above normal Local Housing Allowance limits. 9 What is the difference between exempt and specified accommodation? Specified accommodation is the wider group of supported housing whose rent is still met through Housing Benefit rather than Universal Credit. Exempt accommodation is one type within it. The new licensing regime will apply to supported exempt accommodation that matches the specified accommodation definition. 2 Who will need a supported housing licence? The person managing or in control of supported exempt accommodation will need a licence for each licensing district they operate in. The licence will list every address they are authorised to run. Some services are exempt, including almshouses, commissioned domestic abuse services and certain council-managed accommodation. 2 When does supported housing licensing start? No start date has been set. Government expects to consult on draft regulations in late 2026, and licensing is expected to begin at some point in 2027. 2 , 3 What are the National Supported Housing Standards? They are national standards for the support provided in supported housing in England, built on five principles: person-centred, respectful, safe and responsive, effective, and well-led. The six standards cover person-centred support, empowerment, environment, staff and safeguarding, local need, and a statement of purpose. 2 Will licensing affect Housing Benefit? Yes. Government will amend Housing Benefit regulations so that enhanced Housing Benefit in England is linked to the licensing regime. Plans for new definitions of care, support and supervision have been paused. 2 , 3 What is a managing agent in supported housing? A managing agent is an organisation that manages supported housing day to day, often in properties leased from a Registered Provider, and frequently delivers or arranges the support. The Registered Provider stays accountable as landlord. What is transitional supported housing? Transitional supported housing offers support for a set period, generally six months to two years, often after homelessness, domestic abuse or another crisis. The aim is to help residents move on to independent living. 7 Key dates How we got here, and what comes next. From a non-statutory statement of expectations to a national licensing regime. 20 Oct 2020 National Statement of Expectations Government sets out non-statutory guidance on what good supported housing looks like. 6 Mar 2021 Birmingham charter and quality standards Birmingham, with more than 20,000 units of exempt accommodation, launches a residents' charter and provider quality standards. 10 Oct 2022 Select committee: "a complete mess" MPs call for national standards and council enforcement powers. 8 2022 to 2025 Supported Housing Improvement Programme £20 million for councils to inspect, review support and scrutinise claims. 7 29 Jun 2023 The Act receives Royal Assent Powers for national standards, local licensing and local strategies. 1 16 Apr 2026 Government response published Standards, licence conditions and the Housing Benefit link confirmed. 2 Late 2026 Consultation on draft regulations Expected before regulations are laid in Parliament. 2 31 Mar 2027 Local supported housing strategies due Every local housing authority in England must publish one. 3 2027 Licensing expected to begin Date to be confirmed in regulations. 3 Glossary Supported housing terms, defined. 22 terms you will meet in contracts, audits and the new regulations. Supported exempt accommodation (SEA) Supported housing that qualifies as exempt accommodation for Housing Benefit, so rent can be paid above Local Housing Allowance levels. Exempt accommodation Housing Benefit term for accommodation provided by a housing association, registered charity, voluntary organisation or certain councils that also provide the resident with care, support or supervision. Specified accommodation The wider group of supported housing whose housing costs are met through Housing Benefit rather than Universal Credit. Exempt accommodation sits within it. Enhanced Housing Benefit Housing Benefit paid above Local Housing Allowance levels for exempt accommodation. It will be linked to holding a licence. Registered Provider (RP) A social landlord registered with the Regulator of Social Housing, such as a housing association. Managing agent An organisation that manages supported housing day to day, often in homes leased from a Registered Provider, and often delivers the support. Support provider The organisation that delivers the care, support or supervision to residents. It may or may not be the landlord. Licence holder Under the new regime, the person managing or in control of supported housing in a licensing district. They must pass a fit and proper person test. Licensing authority The local housing authority that will issue supported housing licences for its district. Fit and proper person test A check on whether a licence applicant is suitable. It will extend to directors, partners and nominated individuals. National Supported Housing Standards National standards for the support provided in supported housing in England. Meeting them will be a licence condition. National Statement of Expectations Non-statutory government guidance from October 2020 on what good supported housing looks like. Supported Housing (Regulatory Oversight) Act 2023 The Act giving government powers to set national standards, introduce licensing and require local supported housing strategies. Local supported housing strategy A plan each local housing authority in England must publish by 31 March 2027, covering current supply and future need. Care, support or supervision The help a resident must receive for accommodation to be exempt. Plans to define it more tightly have been paused. Transitional supported housing Supported housing for a set period, generally six months to two years, aimed at helping residents move on to independent living. Move-on The planned move from supported housing into more independent accommodation, and the support that prepares for it. Support needs assessment A record of a resident's support needs, completed after move-in and kept current. Licensing will require one within four weeks of move-in. Support plan The goals agreed with a resident to meet their assessed needs, and how they will be supported to reach them. Risk assessment A record of risks to and from a resident, each scored, usually by likelihood and severity, and reviewed regularly. Risk management plan (RMP) The actions agreed to reduce a risk that scores high enough to need one. Support session A recorded contact where support is delivered, ideally linked to a goal in the support plan. Sources Where our information comes from. Primary sources first. Checked 12 October 2026. Supported Housing (Regulatory Oversight) Act 2023 legislation.gov.uk · Royal Assent 29 June 2023 Supported housing regulation: consultation, government response MHCLG and DWP, GOV.UK · 16 April 2026, updated 19 June 2026 Key changes to how supported housing regulations will be implemented Homeless Link · 28 April 2026 Supported Housing (Regulatory Oversight) Act explainer Homeless Link Supported housing in focus: what the 2023 Act means for landlords and care providers Trowers & Hamlins · July 2026 Supported housing: National Statement of Expectations MHCLG, GOV.UK · 20 October 2020 Supported Housing Improvement Programme prospectus MHCLG, GOV.UK · 2022, withdrawn July 2025 Exempt Accommodation: Third Report of Session 2022–23 Levelling Up, Housing and Communities Committee · October 2022 Housing Benefit and Universal Credit (Supported Accommodation) (Amendment) Regulations 2014 legislation.gov.uk · SI 2014/771 New charter of rights and quality standards for exempt supported housing BVSC and Birmingham City Council · March 2021 Supported Housing (Regulatory Oversight) Act 2023: LGA consultation response Local Government Association · 2025 Want to know how your files measure up? ## Supported Housing Licensing Explained (2026 Update)
Source: https://supportaudit.co.uk/resources/supported-housing-licensing/

Supported Housing Licensing Explained (2026 Update) Skip to content SEA Audit Support Audit home Audits Use cases Resources About Book a call Book a call Home Audits Use cases Resources About Book a call Book a discovery call Book a discovery call contact@supportaudit.co.uk Home / Resources / Licensing guide Guide · Regulation Supported housing licensing explained. What the Supported Housing (Regulatory Oversight) Act 2023 means for Registered Providers, managing agents and support providers: the new standards, who will need a licence, the link to Housing Benefit, and what to do now. By Jamie McCollin , founder, Support Audit Published 8 October 2026 Last reviewed 12 October 2026 12 minute read Contents Key takeaways What the 2023 Act does Why it was introduced The National Supported Housing Standards Who will need a licence Which services are exempt Licensing and Housing Benefit Landlord, agent or support provider? When licensing starts What to do now Questions Sources Contents Key takeaways What the 2023 Act does The standards Who needs a licence Housing Benefit When it starts What to do now Sources Key takeaways Supported exempt accommodation in England will need a local licence, expected from 2027. Meeting the National Supported Housing Standards will be a licence condition, except for most commissioned services. Enhanced Housing Benefit will be linked to holding a licence. Needs assessments within four weeks of move-in will be a licence condition. Draft regulations are expected for consultation in late 2026. Now is the time to get resident files in order. What does the Supported Housing (Regulatory Oversight) Act 2023 do? The Supported Housing (Regulatory Oversight) Act 2023 gives the government powers to regulate supported exempt accommodation in England. It received Royal Assent on 29 June 2023. 1 It has three main strands: National Supported Housing Standards for the support provided to residents. A local licensing regime , run by local housing authorities, for those managing supported exempt accommodation, with compliance with the standards as a licence condition. Local supported housing strategies , which every local housing authority must publish to set out current supply and future need. The Act also created a national Supported Housing Advisory Panel. The powers are being brought in through regulations, which is why the detail has taken time to settle. 1 , 5 Why was it introduced? Supported exempt accommodation grew quickly in some areas, and so did concerns about quality and value for money. In October 2022 the Levelling Up, Housing and Communities Committee described the system as "a complete mess", and called for national standards and enforcement powers for councils. 8 Some councils were already acting. Birmingham, which had more than 20,000 units of supported exempt accommodation, launched a residents' charter and provider quality standards in March 2021. 10 The government's £20 million Supported Housing Improvement Programme then funded councils from 2022 to 2025 to inspect properties, review residents' support and scrutinise Housing Benefit claims. 7 The reforms are meant to make sure supported housing delivers the support people need. For providers, the test will be whether their records show it. Support Audit What are the National Supported Housing Standards? The National Supported Housing Standards set out what good support looks like. They rest on five principles: person-centred, respectful, safe and responsive, effective, and well-led . The government response of 16 April 2026 confirmed six standards. A proposed seventh, the responsible person standard, was dropped. 2 Standard What it expects Person-centred support Needs assessments, tailored support plans and consistent support. Advocates can help co-produce plans. Empowerment Residents involved in developing the service, informed about their support and able to use clear complaints procedures. Environment Support in a clean, comfortable setting, with risk management, managed referrals and a way to report repairs. Staff and safeguarding Trained, DBS-checked staff in sufficient numbers, with poor performance addressed. Local need Consultation with local partners, links to local services and fit with the local strategy. Applies once strategies are published. Statement of purpose A clear ethos, aims, outcomes and partnerships, reviewed every year. What this means for resident files Person-centred support, empowerment, environment, and staff and safeguarding can all be evidenced, or not, from what is in a resident's file. That is where licensing teams are likely to look first. See what a good support file contains . Who will need a supported housing licence? A licence will be needed for all supported exempt accommodation that matches the Housing Benefit definition of specified accommodation. It must be obtained by the person managing or in control of the properties, in each licensing district where they operate. Each licence will list the addresses the holder is authorised to run. 2 Licence conditions confirmed in the government response include: 2 A fit and proper person test , extended to directors, partners and nominated individuals, with an enhanced test where residents are vulnerable. Accommodation meeting existing property standards, such as the Decent Homes Standard or the Housing Health and Safety Rating System. CQC registration where any care is provided. A needs assessment within four weeks of a resident moving in. A suitability condition for service managers. Compliance with the National Supported Housing Standards, for non-commissioned services. There will be no extra local conditions. Licence conditions will be the same nationwide, with guidance to promote consistent decisions. Fees will be set to cover costs only. 2 , 3 Which services are exempt from licensing? The government response lists services that will not need a licence, including: 2 Ministry of Justice-commissioned accommodation for people leaving custody. Supported housing with at least one Ofsted-regulated bed for residents up to 25. Accommodation managed or controlled by a local authority, with support commissioned by the authority or another public body. Commissioned domestic abuse services. Age-restricted housing for over-55s regulated by the Regulator of Social Housing, including extra care. Almshouses. Commissioned services that do need a licence will not have to meet the standards as a licence condition. Instead, commissioners are expected to commission support in line with the standards. 2 , 3 What does licensing mean for Housing Benefit? The government will amend Housing Benefit regulations to link enhanced Housing Benefit in England to the licensing regime. 2 In practice, accommodation that should be licensed but isn't is likely to lose access to rent above Local Housing Allowance levels. Providers found in breach and put on notice to improve will have at least three months to put things right. 2 Proposals for new definitions of care, support and supervision, and a minimum threshold for support, have been paused until licensing is in place. 2 , 3 Who is responsible: landlord, managing agent or support provider? Many supported housing arrangements involve a Registered Provider as landlord, a managing agent and sometimes a separate support provider. The government response says the support standards can be met in full by the support provider, while the housing elements fall to the licence holder through other conditions. Where one organisation provides both housing and support, it needs both in place. 2 Homeless Link notes that clarity on who holds the licence where several parties are involved is still limited. Applicants are encouraged to speak to their licensing authority, and the government plans to publish illustrative case studies. 3 Whatever the final position, each party will want evidence that the support recorded in resident files meets the standards. When will supported housing licensing start? No commencement date has been set. The government expects to consult on draft regulations in late 2026, then lay them before Parliament. Licensing is expected to begin at some point in 2027. 2 , 3 Date Milestone 29 June 2023 Act receives Royal Assent 2025 Consultation on standards, licensing and Housing Benefit 16 April 2026 Government response published (updated 19 June 2026) Late 2026 Consultation on draft regulations expected 31 March 2027 Local supported housing strategies due 2027 Licensing expected to begin The government is not introducing a planning use class for supported housing for now. The Act requires a review after three years. 2 What should providers do now? Regulations are not final, but the direction is clear. These steps are worth taking whatever the final detail: Map your arrangements. List every property, who manages it, who delivers support and which licensing district it sits in. Check needs assessments are prompt. Look at how long after move-in assessments are completed. Four weeks will be the licence condition. Link support plans to needs. Every goal should follow from an assessed need, and be agreed with the resident. Make support visible in session notes. Notes should show what support was given towards which goal, not only that contact happened. Close the loop on risk. Every risk that needs a plan should have a current, dated risk management plan. Hold reviews on time. Reviews at 3, 6 and 9 months, signed and dated by the resident and staff. Get an independent view. A Mock Audit shows what a licensing team or Registered Provider would find, while there is still time to fix it. Questions Do Registered Providers need a supported housing licence? Registered Providers are not exempt as a category. A licence is needed by whoever manages or controls supported exempt accommodation, unless the service falls into one of the listed exemptions. Will there be one licence per property? No. Licences will be held per licensing district and list every address the holder is authorised to run, so most organisations will need one licence per area. Will there be a minimum number of support hours? Not yet. Plans for a minimum threshold for care and support have been paused until licensing is in place. Some Registered Providers already set their own minimum in their agreements with managing agents. Does this apply in Scotland and Wales? Licensing and the standards apply in England. The government has said it will not link Housing Benefit to statutory frameworks in Scotland and Wales. JM Jamie McCollin Founder of Support Audit, with a background in housing, property management and compliance, and hands-on experience auditing resident support files in supported exempt accommodation. Regulations are not yet final, and we update this page when they change. Are your files licence-ready? ## What a Good Resident Support File Contains | Support Audit
Source: https://supportaudit.co.uk/resources/resident-support-file/

What a Good Resident Support File Contains | Support Audit Skip to content SEA Audit Support Audit home Audits Use cases Resources About Book a call Book a call Home Audits Use cases Resources About Book a call Book a discovery call Book a discovery call contact@supportaudit.co.uk Home / Resources / Support file guide Guide · Practice What a good resident support file contains. A document-by-document guide for support teams and managers in supported housing: what each record is for, what auditors look for, the gaps we see most often, and what good looks like. By Jamie McCollin , founder, Support Audit Published 8 October 2026 Last reviewed 12 October 2026 10 minute read Contents Key takeaways What is a resident support file? The ten core documents Evidencing support against goals Risk scoring and plans Reviews at 3, 6 and 9 months Missed sessions The gaps we see most Self-check Sources Key takeaways A good file tells one story: assessed needs, goals that follow from them, support that works towards those goals, and reviews that check progress. Every core document should be complete, signed and dated by the resident and staff. Session notes should record support given towards a goal, not just that contact happened. If it isn't written down, an auditor or licensing team will treat it as not done. What is a resident support file? A resident support file is the set of records kept for one person living in supported housing. It shows why they were offered a place, what support they need, what has been agreed with them, what support has actually been given, and how risks are being managed. It is the main evidence a Registered Provider, council or licensing team will use to judge whether support is real and effective. The National Supported Housing Standards make this more important. Person-centred support, for example, expects needs assessments, tailored support plans and consistent support, and licensing will require a needs assessment within four weeks of move-in. 1 What documents should a resident support file contain? Forms differ between providers, but most files should contain these ten core documents. Always audit against your own forms and thresholds first. Document What it is for What good looks like 1. Referral form Why the resident was referred and by whom Every question answered, source of referral clear, signed and dated 2. Admission or sign-up form The start of the tenancy and what the resident was told Complete, signed and dated on the move-in day 3. Licence or occupancy agreement The legal basis of the occupation Correct landlord or agent name, address and rent, signed by both parties 4. Support needs assessment The resident's support needs Completed within four weeks of move-in, needs described in the resident's situation, updated when things change 5. Support plan Goals agreed with the resident Each goal follows from an assessed need, is specific to the person and is agreed with them 6. Risk assessment Risks to and from the resident Each risk scored and described, consistent with what the rest of the file says 7. Risk management plans How higher risks will be reduced A current plan for every risk above your threshold, with named actions 8. Session notes The support actually given Regular, dated, linked to a goal, showing what the resident did and what happens next 9. Reviews Progress against the plan and risks At 3, 6 and 9 months, signed by the resident and staff, with goals updated 10. Exit or move-on form How and why the stay ended Completed whenever a resident leaves, with the outcome and forwarding details How do you evidence support against goals? The strongest files make a clear chain from need to evidence. An auditor should be able to follow it for every goal: Need Assessed in the needs assessment Goal Agreed in the support plan Action Support given in a session Evidence Recorded in the note, with progress Here is the same session recorded two ways, for a resident whose goal is to build independent living skills: Weak note "Met with resident. All fine. No issues." Shows contact, but no support, no goal and no progress. Strong note "45-minute session. Goal 2, independent living: supported the resident to use the washing machine for the first time. Completed a wash with prompting. Next week: try without prompting." Names the goal, the support, the outcome and the next step. If no session notes evidence work on a goal during the review period, say so plainly in the review and decide whether the goal is still right. How should risks be scored, and when is a risk management plan needed? Most risk assessments score each risk by likelihood multiplied by severity , each on a scale of 1 to 5. Use your own matrix and bands. A common banding looks like this: Score Band Typical response 1 to 4 Low Monitor through normal support 5 to 9 Medium Risk management plan with clear actions 10 to 16 High Risk management plan, closer review, escalation where needed 20 to 25 Critical Immediate action and escalation under your policy Two checks catch most problems: does every risk above your threshold have a current, dated plan, and do the scores match what the rest of the file describes? What should happen at 3, 6 and 9-month reviews? Reviews are where the file proves progress. Each review should revisit every goal, record what has changed, update the risk assessment and plans, and be signed and dated by the resident and staff. A review is only needed once a resident has been there long enough, so a resident in their second month should not be marked down for a missing 3-month review. Timing matters A review completed weeks late is one of the most common reasons a file drops to Amber. Diarise reviews from the move-in date, not from the last review. How should missed sessions be recorded? A missed appointment is not a failure in itself. Not recording it, or not following it up, is. A good file shows the missed session, the attempts made to re-arrange it, and escalation under your process if contact cannot be made. What are the most common gaps in support files? Needs assessments completed weeks after move-in. Generic support goals copied between residents. Session notes that show contact but not support. Weeks with no recorded support. Higher-scoring risks without a risk management plan. Risk scores that contradict the narrative in the file. Reviews completed late, or not signed by the resident. Licence agreements in the wrong name or with the wrong rent. Missed sessions with no follow-up. No exit form when a resident leaves. Self-check: is this file audit-ready? Pick one resident file and work through the list. It takes about ten minutes. 0 / 12 Tick each item that is true for the file in front of you. Reset Referral form complete, signed and dated Admission form signed on the move-in day Licence in the right name, with the right address and rent Needs assessment completed within four weeks of move-in Every support goal follows from an assessed need Goals are specific to this resident, not copied Every risk is scored, and the scores match the file A current plan for every risk above your threshold Support recorded every week of the review period Each session note names a goal and the progress made Missed sessions recorded and followed up Reviews on time, signed by the resident and staff Sources Supported housing regulation: consultation, government response MHCLG and DWP · 16 April 2026, updated 19 June 2026 Supported housing: National Statement of Expectations MHCLG · 20 October 2020 Key changes to how supported housing regulations will be implemented Homeless Link · 28 April 2026 This guide reflects good practice in supported housing auditing. Always follow your own policies, forms and the requirements of your Registered Provider or commissioner. JM Jamie McCollin Founder of Support Audit, with a background in housing, property management and compliance, and hands-on experience auditing resident support files in supported exempt accommodation. Want a second pair of eyes? We will audit a sample of your files to this standard and show you exactly what to fix. ## About Support Audit | Independent Supported Housing Audits
Source: https://supportaudit.co.uk/about/

About Support Audit | Independent Supported Housing Audits Skip to content SEA Audit Support Audit home Audits Use cases Resources About Book a call Book a call Home Audits Use cases Resources About Book a call Book a discovery call Book a discovery call contact@supportaudit.co.uk Home / About and approach About and approach Independent. Evidence-led. On your side. Support Audit exists to find the gaps in resident support files before anyone else does, and to show teams exactly how to close them. Here is who we are and how we work. In short Who is behind Support Audit? Support Audit is an independent audit service for supported housing in England, founded by Jamie McCollin. It combines hands-on experience of auditing resident support files with a structured audit system that checks every file the same way, and an auditor who reads every file, makes every judgement and sets every grade. The founder Built by someone who knows housing from the inside, and knows your staff are stretched. [Founder photo] Jamie McCollin, founder Jamie's background spans housing, property management and compliance, with qualifications across property and health and safety. He has hands-on experience auditing resident support files in supported exempt accommodation, working with managing agents to improve their recording after each audit. He started Support Audit because the same gaps kept appearing, and because providers kept asking the same question: what does good actually look like? Every report we write answers that question. Book a call with Jamie What we stand for Four principles in every audit. Evidence first Every finding names the document and the date. If something isn't in the file, we record it as not seen. Nothing is assumed and nothing is invented. Constructive The point is improvement. Every issue comes with an example of what good looks like, and strengths are named as specifically as gaps. A person decides Our system checks. An experienced auditor reads the whole file, sets every grade and explains the reason for it. Confidential Resident records are special category data. We handle them that way from transfer to deletion. Our method Consistent checks. Human judgement. A structured audit system makes every check consistent and thorough. An experienced auditor makes it fair. Here is exactly who does what. What our audit system checks Checks every file against the same checklist Flags missing signatures, dates and documents Calculates review due dates and weekly support hours Matches session notes to support goals Brings the evidence together for the auditor What the auditor does Reviews every flag and every judgement Reads the file as a whole, in context Sets the final grade and writes the reason Names the strengths and the next steps Talks it through with your team How we write Plain, specific and fair. Our reports are written to be used by support workers, not filed by managers. UK English, written the way an experienced auditor speaks Every issue names the document, the date and what is wrong Every issue includes a short example of what good looks like Strengths drawn from the documents, never generic praise Gaps stated plainly: "No session notes evidence work on this goal" Data protection How we handle resident data. Resident support files contain special category data under UK GDPR. These commitments apply to every audit. 01 Agreed before anything is shared A data processing agreement and retention period are agreed with you before any files are sent. 02 Only what is needed We request only the files and the review period in scope, and nothing else. 03 Secure transfer and storage Files are shared through a secure transfer and stored with access limited to the audit team. 04 Deleted on schedule Resident data is deleted at the end of the agreed retention period, and we confirm it in writing. 05 Not used to train AI Resident data is used only to deliver your audit. It is never used to train AI models. 06 Registered Support Audit is registered with the Information Commissioner's Office. Registration number: [ICO number]. 07 Who to ask Data protection questions, subject access requests and DPA queries go to dpo@supportaudit.co.uk . Resident files are sent to audit@supportaudit.co.uk , never to a personal address. Privacy and terms The small print, kept short. Privacy notice When you contact us, we use your name, organisation and contact details only to respond to your enquiry and arrange a call. We don't sell or share them. [Full privacy notice to be added.] Terms of business Every audit is agreed in writing before it starts, including scope, fee, timescale and data handling. [Full terms to be added.] Not legal advice Our guides summarise published government material to help providers prepare. They are not legal advice. Let's talk about your files.
